title: White Rice with Vegetables and Gravy, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked with vegetables and gravy, with added fat, is a hearty dish popular in many cuisines. The rice provides carbohydrate energy, vegetables add vitamins and minerals, and the fat makes the meal more caloric and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Combining rice with vegetables increases fiber and B‑vitamin content.
Gravy is often made from broth, tomatoes or cream, giving the dish aroma and juiciness.
Adding fat (oil or butter) improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
Traditionally the dish is served hot as a side or a main course.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice is a quick source of carbohydrates that rapidly replenish muscle glycogen stores.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and magnesium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Fat for nutrient absorption
items.content: Fat aids the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and makes the dish more satiating.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from vegetables promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Balanced macronutrient profile
items.content: The mix of carbs, a modest amount of protein from vegetables, and fat makes the dish suitable for post‑exercise recovery.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat increases the dish’s energy density, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Gravy often contains salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to certain vegetables or the type of fat (e.g., dairy butter).

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a side to meat, fish, or as a standalone meal. Garnish with fresh herbs, spices, or a squeeze of lemon to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.
